Neonatal development in Homo sapiens begins with a newborn typically measuring approximately 60 cm [Lb = approximately 60 cm] in head-feet length at birth, a value that reflects the constraints of pelvic architecture and the altricial-like state of human infants relative to other primates. The typical birth mass is around 3313 grams [Wwb = around 3313 grams], which, while modest compared to the maternal body mass, represents a substantial energetic investment in a large-brained, slow-maturing neonate. Weaning, marking the transition from complete nutritional dependence on maternal milk to a mixed diet, occurs at around 665 days since birth [tx = around 665 days since birth] in traditional subsistence populations, though considerable variation exists across c at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]ultures. This protracted suckling period is an adaptation that supports the slow neurological development characteristic of the species. Following weaning, the juvenile period extends for several years, during which the individual grows steadily toward the ultimate head-feet length of 165 cm [Li = 165 cm] attained in healthy adults, though final stature is influenced by genetic and environmental factors.

Puberty in humans initiates a pronounced transformation in body composition and linear growth velocity. At this stage, the average head-feet length reaches approximately 160 cm [Lp = approximately 160 cm] for females, who typically enter puberty earlier than males, and the corresponding wet weight at puberty averages 48 kilograms [Wwp = 48 kilograms]. This period of rapid somatic change is under tight endocrine control at a core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], and the time since birth at puberty for females is generally around 4685 days [tp = around 4685 days], whereas males tend to mature later, with puberty occurring at roughly 5500 days since birth [tp = roughly 5500 days since birth]. The delay in male maturation is thought to reflect the extended growth period needed to achieve a larger adult body size, which confers competitive advantages in intrasexual selection. The onset of reproductive capacity does not immediately follow puberty; a period of adolescent subfertility, known as adolescent sterility, typically lasts for one to three years after the first menstrual cycle or first ejaculation, representing an adaptive interval during which the individual completes skeletal growth and acquires necessary somatic resources before undertaking the energetic demands of gestation and lactation.

Gestation in Homo sapiens is notably prolonged compared to many other primates of similar body mass, with a standard gestation time of approximately 305 days [tg = approximately 305 days] at the internal body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This extended intrauterine development is essential for permitting the substantial brain growth that distinguishes humans from other hominids, even though human neonates are born at a relatively altricial neurological stage compared to other anthropoids. The trade-off between gestational length, neonatal brain size, and the biomechanical constraints of bipedal pelvic morphology is a central theme in human evolutionary biology. Following parturition, the wet weight at weaning is documented to be approximately 11750 g [Wwx = approximately 11750 g]rams, representing roughly a 3.5-fold increase from the birth mass over the nursing period, which is comparatively modest among primates given the extended lactation duration. The energetic burden of lactation on the mother is substantial, and the transition to solid foods is gradual, with complementary feeding typically beginning around six months postpartum in most cultures, although complete weaning often occurs much later as reflected in the tx value.

Maximum lifespan in humans is exceptionally long in mammalian terms, with reliably documented maximum longevity reaching about 85 years [am = about 85 years] under modern conditions, when measured at a stable core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This extreme longevity is accompanied by a unique life-history pattern characterized by a prolonged post-reproductive period, the evolution of which has been attributed to the grandmother hypothesis, wherein older females enhance the survival of their grandchildren through resource provisioning and childcare. The daily energetic requirements of adult males are considerable; the adult male maintenance intake, measured as the daily caloric demand required to sustain basal metabolic processes and routine activity at 37 °C [T = 37 °C], is on the order of 8.4 million joules per day . This substantial energy requirement is met through a varied omnivorous diet and is facilitated by complex food-processing behaviors, including cooking, which increases the net energy yield of ingested foods and is considered a key innovation in human evolution.

Ultimate wet weight in humans is subject to considerable sexual dimorphism, with females typically reaching an asymptotic mass of approximately 68 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 68 kilograms], whereas adult males attain a higher ultimate wet weight of about 80 kilograms [Wwi = about 80 kilograms]. This dimorphism emerges during the adolescent growth spurt under the influence of sex steroids, particularly testosterone, which promotes greater muscle mass accretion in males. The maximum reproduction rate, defined as the highest possible frequency of live births under optimal conditions, is approximately one birth per thousand days, equivalent to an interbirth interval of just under three years, when measured at a core temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This low reproductive rate is typical of a slow life-history strategy characterized by high investment in individual offspring, large body size, and extended parental care. The combination of a very long lifespan, late age at first reproduction, small litter size typically limited to a single offspring, and intensive biparental care places humans at the extreme slow end of the mammalian life-history continuum, with profound consequences for population dynamics and social organization.
